- **Targets.** Before the stream opens, the node attaches its own session to the browser target and calls `Target.setDiscoverTargets` and `Target.getTargets` on it with ids of its own. Neither the session nor its messages ever reach the page. From then on it knows every target's URL and opener. A target on an inheriting URL (`about:blank`, `about:srcdoc`, none) is protected when it was protected before or when its opener is protected or unknown, so a blank popup that seven opens counts as seven. On a page session, the main frame's `url` and `securityOrigin` (`Page.frameNavigated`, `Page.documentOpened`) and the default context's `origin` (`Runtime.executionContextCreated`) count too, and so does the main frame of a `Page.getFrameTree` or `Page.getResourceTree` answer, which the page then gets as a refusal. A Chrome error page's main frame is not counted this way; the error-page rule below covers it. For the default context's `origin` (slicc-browsers ≥ 1.37.0, `contextOrigin`), any value that starts with `about:` in any case, other than exactly `about://`, protects the page, such as `about:blank`, `about:newtab` or `ABOUT://`. The exact `about://` is the opaque origin of that rule, but the node still judges it as the `chrome://` URL it names, so a page whose default context reports `about://` is protected too: a browser that reports `about://` for its blank pages has them refused. `://` and ordinary origins are judged as before.
- **URLs slicc can't parse** count as protected wherever the node judges a URL the browser will load or has loaded. Chrome's parser and the node's (WHATWG) disagree at the edges: Chrome loads `http://exa mple.sliccy.ai/` as `http://exa%20mple.sliccy.ai/`, a `sliccy.ai` host that gets seven's cookies, and, in some versions, `http://<U+200D>.sliccy.ai/` as `http://xn--1ug.sliccy.ai/`, and the node's parser rejects all of those forms. On top of the WHATWG parse, the node checks a host the way its parser did up to whatwg-url 0.6.2: invalid UTF-8 is replaced with U+FFFD, and a host with an `xn--` label must pass IDNA with STD3 rules and hold only code points assigned in Unicode 15.0 that aren't noncharacters. IDNA and the node's own check both refuse the 66 noncharacters. The Unicode 15.0 table is frozen in `internal/protect/unicode15.go` and doesn't follow Go's or x/text's Unicode version: `node scripts/unicode15.mjs > internal/protect/unicode15.go` regenerates it from `https://www.unicode.org/Public/15.0.0/ucd/DerivedAge.txt` (sha256 `7570877e0fa197c45338f7c41a02636da4e14c8dba6a3611a01cd30bf329d5ca`, which the script checks), and `TestProtectUnicode15TableIsFrozen` pins the file's hash, so moving the freeze to another Unicode version is a reviewed change to the script, the hash and the decision table. `test/integration/testdata/whatwgurl/decisions.txt` holds the node's decisions on 5,616 URLs, and `TestProtectURLDecisionTable` fails when a parser, Go or x/net update changes any of them. So a command whose destination doesn't parse (`url` of `Target.createTarget`, `Page.navigate`, `Fetch.continueRequest`, `Network.continueInterceptedRequest`, `Network.loadNetworkResource` and `PWA.launch`, `installUrlOrOrigin` of `PWA.install`, the `url` of a cookie command or any of the `urls` of `Network.getCookies` and `Page.getCookies`, and a history entry's `url` or `userTypedURL`) is refused with `slicc: refused: slicc can't parse this URL, so it could be a protected page`. An empty URL is fine (`Target.createTarget` with `url: ""` opens `about:blank`). On the browser's side, a target, a main frame's `securityOrigin`, an execution context's `origin`, a request or WebSocket, and a service worker whose URL doesn't parse are protected like seven's: left out of listings (see Listing), not attachable, detached, hidden, their document loads failed and their requests stripped. The opaque origins `null` and `://` are not affected; `about://` is not treated as opaque here (see *Targets*). A `blob:null/…` URL (a blob made on an opaque origin, such as a `data:` page or a sandboxed frame) is: its inner `null/…` doesn't parse, and slicc can't name the blob's creator, so it is protected too. URLs the node only reads, such as storage keys and script URLs, are unaffected. In what the page gets, a URL that doesn't parse is cut whole (to an empty string), because it has no origin to keep. The cost: a page on a host that Chrome accepts and WHATWG doesn't (an invalid `xn--` label, a joiner such as U+200D, a space or another forbidden code point), and Chrome's error page for one, is cut too, and navigating to it is refused. URLs Chrome rejects as well (`http://[::1`, `http://a:99999/`, `http://1.2.3.4.5/`) lose nothing: Chrome answers `Page.navigate` with `Cannot navigate to invalid URL`, and `Target.createTarget` with a tab that never loads a document.
